utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Registrar, please have the witness brought in. (The witness/accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are resuming the hearing. I should like to say good morning to the interpreters, counsel for the Prosecution, counsel for the Defence, the accused. I should like to point out that the accused, General Blaskic, is here in the capacity of a witness under oath, and he is answering questions by the Prosecutor within the framework of the cross-examination. Before beginning, Mr. Prosecutor, have you thought about the question of the organisation of our work and the possibility of using Rule 71, that is, deposition testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. We have not come to a resolution of that yet. I will be hopefully discussing the issue with the Prosecutor this afternoon or after the session this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. I'm just drawing your attention to the fact that it will be extremely difficult to complete the presentation of evidence before the end of the month of July, and that is why I'm emphasising this matter. In that case, we can go on with Mr. Kehoe, I think, who is doing the cross-examination on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we left off yesterday discussing the three orders that you issued on the 15th and 16th of April, Defence Exhibits 267, 268, and 269. Using your own terminology concerning the HVO as a peasant army, is it your opinion, General, that in dealing with a peasant army, you as a commanding officer have to be more careful or less careful in giving orders to that peasant army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, it is necessary to be careful and to issue orders precisely, and I always did so, endeavouring always when I had occasion to clarify orders to the commanders, to explain what they mean and how the order should be understood and executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is not the question, General Blaskic. Please let's try and answer the question. The question was of a general nature, that is, if you have an army of nonprofessionals, whether the orders have to be specifically oriented towards the protection of civilians. Afterwards, you can justify your answer if you wish to. It is what was said, Mr. Hayman. The question was, when you have a peasant army, a nonprofessional army, shouldn't one, generally speaking, take even greater precautions? Will you please answer the question first? Have you understood the question?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have understood your question, but I wrote down the Prosecutor's question as I received it through the interpretation, and I can answer your question now. Yes, of course, one must pay attention, and I did pay attention to having the orders be concrete and clear and defined according to the targets, that is to say, the objective of each order. Many of the orders that I wrote were quite certainly written for the lowest possible level, so not the corps commander but somebody far below him, so that the order should be completely clear to everybody who was to execute that order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, thank you. Continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In issuing an attack order, an order to attack, would you agree, General, that the care that you must demonstrate must be very high, and would you agree that you must explicitly tell your subordinates to protect civilians during any such attack, given the fact that you're dealing with a peasant army? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know which order of attack you're talking about, Mr. Prosecutor, if you could specify. I'm not sure what order of attack you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about one that is very relevant to our time frame, and that would be Defence Exhibit 299 and Defence Exhibit 300, which are the preparatory attack order and the attack order that you gave for the attack on the Kiseljak area to the Ban Jelacic Brigade. I know that you've seen those before, General, but I ask you to take a look at them once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which exhibit are we talking about, D300?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm going to try to use as many exhibits as possible in unison, Mr. President, to move this along, and I'm looking at Exhibit 299 and 300, which counsel, during the direct examination of the witness, said these are two documents that have to be looked at together. They focus on the attack on Kiseljak on the morning of the 18th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you finished reviewing them again, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we focus on those two documents, I ask you once again, do you agree with the general principle that a commander who issues an attack order to a peasant army, as you have described the HVO, must take a greater degree of care to inform that army of its obligations under international humanitarian law to protect civilians?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He must, of course, do that in the time preceding the use of those forces and not at a time when he is issuing that order. Allow me to answer this question by giving an extra clarification. Whenever I was able to, I personally addressed the soldiers that were to go into combat activities and caution them of the need for humane behaviour. Yesterday, I said that the way we were trained in the former JNA, standard orders do not contain a specific paragraph on the protection of civilians. It is a legal obligation which is always implicit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in dealing with your peasant army, you would agree that in the attack order given to the Ban Jelacic Brigade on the 17th of April, 1993, there is no paragraph in either of these documents informing your subordinates to protect civilians, is there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A paragraph as a paragraph is not there because it wasn't the standard, as I have already said, but allow me to comment on this order for preparation of combat activities. I claim that this was at the level of the commander of a platoon, and in writing this order personally and knowing the kind of soldiers that I was dealing with, I always wrote very precisely in terms of the standards of the commander of a platoon and not the commander of a corps. Point 2 of the document, document 299, Defence Exhibit 299, point 2 states that the mission of the troops is to tie up the forces of the aggressor, and then I go a step further and explain how this should be done, and so you have 2(a), and 2(b), and 2(c), which means that I'm going down to the bottom level to clarify to that commander how he should execute that order, the methods that he is to use, the way he is to do this, in order to direct himself principally towards military targets. If you look at point 5 of this particular order where I tell the commander that when all preparations have been carried out and "when you inform me thereof, then the following command will be issued." In the case of combat activities, this is, once again, an exception or something very rare.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The simple answer to my question is "No. No such provision exists in these two orders"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Listen, we're at the beginning of the cross-examination, and I want to make a very simple point. Mr. Hayman, I must admit that you are right, but you must also recognise that the witness is not providing a direct answer. It was a simple question. The order that we have in front of us and the question was "Were there any specific measures in that order?" I'm going to engage in some pedagogy, which I don't usually do. The witness says, "Yes, but I was addressing myself to the platoon commander," which means not to the troops directly, but then he also adds, "Not only to the platoon commander, but you see A, B, C, and point 5 in which I'm very precise." I'm sorry, but that is not the answer to the question that was put to him. I don't wish to preach, but from time to time, I'm forced to. General Blaskic, you were telling us how you addressed a platoon commander, which means that your answer to the Prosecutor is that you didn't address yourself directly to the peasants, but you are not answering the question, whether you told that platoon commander anything specific and additional with regard to the protection of civilians. That is the point. In B, you are telling the platoon commander to take control of Gomionica, but that is not the answer to the question. The objection of Mr. Hayman is valid, but we must also acknowledge that the witness is not giving precise answers to the questions. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, quite obviously the problem is in the interpretation. The witness never said that he contacted the platoon commander; he said that he ordered the commander of a brigade. But as he did not have a top quality army, he wrote out in detail -- the witness said that he ordered to the commander of a brigade, but as the army was not a top quality army, in the text of the order, he elaborated in detail everything up to the level of a platoon, as if he was addressing a platoon. As if he was addressing the commander of a platoon. So he went to this level for his instructions to be precise. Although he was not duty-bound to do that by the regulations, but he knew the army that he had before him, so that is the way he wrote his orders. So he didn't command the commander of the platoon.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: May I clarify matters, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This order was addressed to the commander of the brigade, and had I worked according to the standards of the former JNA, I would have written this order in much more generalised terms for the commander of the brigade, but as I knew the kind of commander cadres we had and the kind of soldiers we had, in writing this order personally, I went far lower down the hierarchy, and I said that I wrote it with the commander of a platoon in mind. So I wrote it with such great precision and in such concrete terms that there could be no dilemmas in executing this order and no dilemmas as to the objectives. In point 5 of this particular order, I stressed that when all preparations have been carried out, that is, stating your readiness, that another order would arrive. So this is a preparatory order. I should just like to ask, in answer in what the Prosecutor has asked me, Mr. President, according to the standards of the former JNA, and I refer to all the rules and regulations that govern the JNA, there is no point of order for the protection of civilians. There is no specific point there. But in assessing the situation, when the commander receives this kind of order, he must respect the rules on how to conduct fighting in a built-up area. So he must have had that in mind. This is the commander of the brigade in Kiseljak, and he was a trained officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, you see now, the answer is that, according to you, General Blaskic, this order does contain additional precautions regarding the protection of civilians, because you are addressing yourself to a trained commander. Mr. Kehoe, we have taken note of your answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, by your own testimony, after you received Colonel Stewart's letter on the 22nd of April of 1993, you, by your own testimony, then knew that something terrible had happened in Ahmici. I ask you, based on that and based on what you knew that your peasant army had done, did you take additional precautions in giving combat orders to your troops after you learned what had happened to Ahmici? Did you instruct that peasant army to protect the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There are several questions here so, Mr. Prosecutor, can we go there one by one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any way you want, General. I'll make it very simple. Let me start from the beginning. Did you think, after you learned what happened in Ahmici, that you had to be more careful to protect civilians when you issued combat orders?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not only did I think that I should be more careful after having learned what had taken place in Ahmici, but I took several measures, including my public condemnation of the incident, and I was convinced that this position of mine had reached the ears of every soldier and every family in the Lasva pocket, because I appeared on television, and my image was there as well as my voice. But what you're saying here is that you're implying that this was done by the peasants. However, we can put Colonel Stewart's letter on there and see what he has to say about it, what his position is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in the combat orders that you issued after the 22nd of April, 1993, did you include in those combat orders a note of caution to your subordinates to protect civilian lives and civilian property, especially for the Muslims? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course, and I also tasked them in specific orders, but let me just say, Your Honours, the protection of civilians and their property, and let me repeat this, was a legal obligation. The law had to be respected and obeyed by every soldier. I issued a number of orders regarding the protection of civilians, especially Bosniak Muslims in the area controlled by the HVO units. So there were a number of such orders issued regarding both the civilians and their property, including that my subordinates -- so that my direct subordinates would issue further orders down the chain of command in that regard. As far as the combat operations, either defensive or offensive, all these orders would be preceded by preparations. This was standard procedure also in the former JNA. This is the training that we received. This preparation is carried out at several levels, with all the participants in such an operation. One of the points is the assessment of the enemy, assessment of the terrain where the operation is going to be carried out, and within that preparation the civilian targets and civilian objects are defined with respect to the goals of the military operation. So every operation was preceded by such preparation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, my question is very simple. After you learned about Ahmici, did you take additional safeguards in your orders telling your subordinates to protect the Muslim population, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, this question was answered in great detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The objection is sustained. You have asked the question. The witness is entitled to answer in the way he wants to. You may not be satisfied with the answer, Mr. Kehoe, but I believe that the witness has answered the question put to him. It was, "Yes," and, "I did so."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If we could move to the next exhibit, which is 456/93.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: While that's being gotten. Clearly, Mr. President, Mr. Kehoe's technique is to provoke the witness, repeat the question over and over, demand a "Yes" or "No," and he shouldn't be allowed to do so, and we intend to object when he engages in that kind of conduct. We ask the Court's assistance in regulating the cross-examination so that it's fair and reasonable under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, your observation is absolutely superfluous. The assistance of the Chamber is not intended for either party. The Judges are neutral and objective, and I respond to objections as they appear. Just now I can considered your objection valid. I am not here to assist the Defence or the Prosecution but to deal with the problems as they crop up. Very well. Mr. Prosecutor, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like you to take a look at this order, which is 456/93, which has to do with a battle order directed to the commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Of the Prosecution or Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The number of this order on the upper left-hand side is 01, meaning it's coming from you, 6370/93. I think you can take a look at the contents in this order. Will you agree that the date at the top should be the 15th of June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Your Honours, I have not been able to review the entire document, but what I have seen so far, this would not be in -- this could not have happened in 1992. So can I please review the entire document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, you may examine the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President, I agree with the witness that it didn't happen in 1992, that this happened in 1993.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have reviewed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, was this order, in fact, issued in June of 1993 as opposed to 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You, in fact, issued this order; did you not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With the Court's indulgence, if at some point the registrar can correct the date on the English translation to reflect the 15th of June, 1992, with a pencil notation, because it's not clear from the BSC version whether it's '92 or '93.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are against it. In the original there was '92. It was a mistake. It was an error. Let it be reflected that mistakes were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's fine. If the witness says it's 1993, that's the point. That's fine. There is no disagreement on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us not waste any time over this. It is in the record, but the Judges know that this document is dated the 15th of June, 1993. So let us continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, this document was issued or this order was issued almost two months after the events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 4(b) of this order, and we'll read that, in your order of discharging tasks you write: "Secret and safe evacuation of the people and the wounded to the Mravinjac," pardon my pronunciation, "facility, exclusively women, children, and the elderly and the assigning of a group leader to them with the objective of their transfer to the Republic of Croatia." Now, in that particular paragraph, which is then followed by what exactly you want to do, paragraph (c), preventing any surrender to the Muslim forces as well as shelling by mortar rounds, in that paragraph (b) you call for the safeguarding of Bosnian Croat civilians, don't you, because you're talking about the secret and safe evacuation? That's what you want, the secret and safe evacuation of Bosnian Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: These were the civilians who had been surrounded. At that moment, the majority were probably Croats, but I cannot preclude that there were some Muslims or Serbs or whoever else happened to be there. There were mixed marriages, so there could have been some Muslims there too, but I assume that the majority of them were Croats. I had no information who exactly was surrounded there. Point 4 does not refer to the tasks of the unit to whom I'm issuing the order. It would be in point 2 that the tasks would be reflected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, is there anything in this record calling for the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade to protect the Bosnian Muslim population in that area? I'm talking about the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I will give you a direct answer to this question. I am familiar with these events, and the area was surrounded. This is a small area. I can show it on the map. They found themselves in a sandwich between the army of the Republika Srpska and the front lines of the BH army. There were the HVO soldiers and alongside them there were civilians in this encirclement. I did not have information what civilians were involved here, nor did I give it special consideration. I just knew that alongside the soldiers there were civilians encircled there. This order, if compared to the standards of the former JNA, if it were to be translated, it would be a combat order, that is, my task was to issue orders in as short a period of time as possible to the local commander. Had I had technical capabilities, I would have just called him through the communications system without writing an order. Let me just try to comment on point 2. I took all measures to protect the civilians in the encirclements as if I was the commander on the ground who was to carry out this order. Also, it says, "Immediate preparations must be made for pulling out and operations of the following deployed, frontal security, scouts, patrols, units, flank security, security for the main body of the column, and rear security." Point 3 says that after deciding on the direction of the pull-out, forces in front of the front line must be given specific instructions for receiving the units. Then point 4, I laid out very accurately how to carry out the orders from point 2 so that the soldiers -- it would be very clear to the soldiers how to do it. I said that organising a defence of the people should be carried out, and I referred to the "people." So that would be everybody. In (c), I strictly forbid military conscripts to act in contravention of these orders and so on. It's all stated here. Then in (f), the preparations and secrecy. Then in point 5, prevent panic and defeatism, lies, disorders, and prepare all structures for defence and evacuation, and draw up lists of all villagers who were encircled. So I did not say all the Croats, because there were Serbs there in those villages, perhaps even Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am very grateful to you for commenting on the whole combat order, but was that your question, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No. I cannot take your place. You are the accused, and it is up to you to try and defend yourself as you will, but please make an effort. It seems to me that the question was not to know under which conditions, how and when, you made this order, but the question referred to point 4(b), and I think that you answered that question. Perhaps we can go on to the next question, Mr. Kehoe. I think that the witness answered that he wasn't concerned specifically about Croats, that there may have been other people too. You have an additional question to what you have already put?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when, in fact, issuing this order, you told these troops at point 5 in the information and propaganda activity the following: "Impress upon the people and the soldiers the brutality of the aggression of the Muslim Armed Forces and that the only way to prevent a massacre is to fight the enemy and protect our own people and pledge that we will eventually return to our territory. "Do not forget the suffering of the Croats in Travnik, Kakanj, and the struggle HVO soldiers have been waging to defend Croatian territory. "Prevent panic, defeatism, lies, and the spreading of unrest. Prepare all structures for defence and evacuation and draw up lists of all villagers." Did you write that in this order, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what is written in point 5, but the translation of the first paragraph is not good, the one that you read out. The first paragraph in translation does not correspond to the original that I have here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is the translation that was provided by the translation department. I, of course, don't speak the language and must rely on the good services of that office to provide the Chamber with the translations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let us move to a separate topic. Now, General, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we are now rounding off a section, perhaps we could now have a break in accordance with your decision to give a pause after 45 minutes in view of the condition of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but we did envisage a certain amount of flexibility, Mr. Nobilo. Therefore, perhaps Mr. Kehoe could go on with another one or two questions. We can go on until 11.00, and then we will have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, when you wrote these orders and you became a member of the HVO, you had had years of military training, and I believe you had been in the JNA for approximately a little more than eight years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: May I first answer the question regarding years of training behind me? In the former JNA, I completed two years of military secondary school and the military academy. That is all the training that I had behind me. I did not attend any special courses or any additional training, and my command duty was a company commander and deputy battalion commander. That was the highest position that I held in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the JNA was a formidable army and a very large army, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was a bulky army, an army that had its own problems and was engaged in dealing with those problems. It was a big army. It had a large infrastructure which, for a time, was a burden for it. For instance, in my case, out of 600 soldiers, we had to provide 200 for regular guard duty over the infrastructure, so we didn't have enough troops to train.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, it was an army with armed forces with, in addition to infantry, mechanised units, an air force, a navy; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In that army, motorised units started to be introduced, as far as I know, in 1985. Before that, there was the ordinary infantry lacking sufficient means of transport. It had an air force; I don't know at what level of development it was. It had a navy. It had ground troops and the other branches and services of the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This armed forces, the JNA, was grounded on the principle of subordination, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It had a two-fold system: subordination, which implied command duties, and ranks, so that command was based on rank and on position, command positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And subordination in that ranking structure was an intricate part in the JNA and command in the JNA, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the HVO was formed, the HVO followed this same model, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the HVO rejected -- at least that's my personal conviction which can be corroborated by the documents. In its concept of organisation, it rejected everything reminiscent of the JNA, but it didn't have a clear and elaborate model of its own, though it had intended to follow this system of command positions in subordination, which means that there were no ranks and command duties based on ranks up until the signing of the Washington Agreement, that is, in 1994 when ranks started to be introduced in the HVO with the establishment of the army of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can take the break now. I have a few more questions in this area, but we can take a break now. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: A 15-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume the hearing now. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me show you Article 32 on the decree of the armed forces, and I believe that we have that pulled out.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecutor's Exhibit 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Registrar. We are talking about tab 2, page 18, and in that page, I'm referring to Article 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What article is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Article 32, Mr. President. This is part of the decree of the armed forces from the Narodni List.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, do you have Article 32 before you? It's on the page that's tagged with a yellow sticker on top.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could put that on the ELMO and just read that briefly: "Command in the Armed Forces shall be founded on the following fundamental principles: a) unity of command and the obligation to implement the decisions and carry out the command and orders of a superior commander; and b) commanders of the Armed Forces shall be responsible to their superiors for their work, command and control." Now, General, that was a fundamental principle of the former JNA and then had been incorporated into the Narodni List and became a fundamental principle of the HVO as well; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Partially, yes. The basic principles of the former JNA were unity of command, subordination, centralisation, continuity, operationalism, and the secrecy of the command. That is what we were taught at the academy in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whether or not, according to your statement, the HVO had ranks, that principle of subordination was incorporated into the HVO, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Your Honours, this principle was negated by other legal acts in the HVO, such as the rules and regulations and laws on the organisation of the security service, then the military police and the special purpose units, so that other legal acts came into being on the structure of the HVO which vitally upset the principle of unity of command. With the existence of this duality and many lines of command, this principle did not exist for any length of time in the HVO and, as far as I know, up until the Dayton Accords; of that, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you left the JNA in 1991. Up until the time you left the JNA, was there mandatory conscription of the male population into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was the military obligation which men and women had to respond to, as far as I know, although I did not work on tasks of mobilising the civilian population into the ranks of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia. But according to what I know, there was this military obligation for both men and women, for women as well, women conscripts as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was approximately a year's worth of mandatory training; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is not the same as military obligation and training. If we're talking about training, then training in the former Yugoslavia was military service, and military service lasted 12 months for the majority of members, except for the military conscripts who did not want to take up arms, and their military service was somewhat longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this year of military service, did officers such as yourself instruct these conscripts to learn how to take orders?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers were trained in the basics of military action. The commanders of the platoons and squads were trained on how to receive orders and convey orders to their immediate subordinates. The soldiers received orders from their commanders, the commanders of squads or platoons, and would act on those orders. So they had this executive obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A fundamental aspect of the principle of subordination is that soldiers learn and know that they must take orders and follow orders; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In principle that could be so. So it is the duty of the subordinate to carry out the tasks of his superior and to inform him thereof.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, another intricate arm of the military in the former Yugoslavia was the concept of the Territorial Defence which was located on a local area; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The concept of Territorial Defence existed but let me clarify this. It was one of the components of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia, because the armed forces consisted of the JNA and Territorial Defence, but within the composition of Territorial Defence, the core was also the officers cadre and sometimes the units of the JNA themselves. So it wasn't a pure, clear-cut division, the JNA component and the Territorial Defence component, but the core and nucleus of the Territorial Defence was also composed of members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these members of the Territorial Defence receive any training during the course of their service?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Somewhere around 1983, I know well, because at the time I served in a unit of that kind. It was called the 14th Proletarian Infantry Division in Ljubljana in Sentvid. The members of the Territorial Defence, up to the level of battalion, were called up in such a way that once in three years -- once every three years a soldier was duty-bound to attend training which lasted usually seven days. Every year they were called up for the records to be brought up-to-date. But somewhere from 1985 or 1986 onwards, because there were not sufficient financial resources, this system of training was abandoned and the call-ups were far less frequent. For example, at the level of the entire 9th Army, there was just one training exercise in one year at the level of a brigade, a brigade on the offensive and a brigade on the defensive, where the members of the TO were called up. So my answer is as there were less and less financial resources, then the TO members would be called up less and less for training of this kind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any training received in the Territorial Defence in addition to the training that an individual received when he or she was doing their military service?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me clarify matters. It was a military obligation for one and all. After a recruit had served his military service, up to the age of 60 if he was a -- males up to the age of 60 are duty-bound as a member -- as a civilian, but he still has his military obligation to perform and would be called up for military training. But as I say, as the financial resources were lacking in the JNA, who paid for that military training, organised and financed it, then invitations to do this kind of training were less and less frequent. Apart from this type of call-up to training, I do not know of any other forms in which those members were trained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, my question was very simple and let me read it to you again, and it was this: Was any training received in the Territorial Defence in addition to the training that an individual received when he or she was doing his or her military service?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is precisely what the witness said exhaustively in his previous answer. He said recruits did a year of military service and then were later called up to do training from time to time but less and less as there was less and less finance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Move on, Mr. Prosecutor. The witness has already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within this area of the military you also had a reserve officers corps as well.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I worked for three years and I trained and educated them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, General, that within the former Yugoslavia, a large percentage of the population have had military training in some degree or another? Would that be an accurate statement, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could only say, in answer to that question, that all young men, that is to say, males who were military-able men and able physically to do their military service were called up to do so, once they had reached the age of 18 and going on to the age of 27. Now, what percentage that was of how many military-able men there were, I can say from my experience because I worked in this here, that there were many recruits that had limited military capability, but they did do their regular military service, that is to say, once in their life time they did indeed spend one year doing military service if they were military-able men. Now, what the percentage was, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in summary on this area, for all of those men and women that you have been discussing, were they all instructed in the need and the requirement to follow the orders of their superiors?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All men who did their military service were trained and instructed in the need to follow orders, those that did their military service. Women, in a brief period of time, it was an experimental phase, I think it lasted for one year whereby they did their military service, that for each republic there were 30 females per republic. After that that was given up. That experiment was abandoned, and women were no longer called to the army to do their military service, but as civilians they were the protagonists of the military obligation, that is to say, in a general war they would be duty-bound to comply with the order for general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us shift gears and topics, General, and talk about your military service. Correct me if I'm wrong, but I believe you noted, during your direct-examination, that you received your commission in 1993 and received your first assignment to Ljubljana; is that right? Excuse me, 1983, I apologise, and received your first assignment in Ljubljana?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your assignment in Ljubljana within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was in Ljubljana, in Sentvid. I worked there at the 14th Proletarian Infantry Regiment, the commander of the first instructors platoon, cadets platoon for reserve officers of the JNA. The JNA, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were your superior officers? Who were they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My immediate superior officer, the commander of the cadet instructors company, was Alojz Vertic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a Muslim, a Serb, or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was a Slovene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Above Mr. Vertic -- who was above him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Above him was the commander of the 14th proletarian regiment, Mr. Jovo Uzelac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, with regard to mister -- I'm trying to get the spelling here. What ethnic group was this individual?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not quite sure there. I can only suppose that he belonged -- he was either a Serb or he was a Yugoslav by way of nationality. He either declared himself as a Serb or he declared himself as a Yugoslav. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him after the war broke out, what side he was fighting for, if any?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what happened to him. I haven't had -- I don't know what happened to him as of 1991, because I went to another garrison and I have no information as to what had happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, what was your next assignment after this Ljubljana assignment?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After my assignment in Ljubljana you mean, my service in Ljubljana?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was assigned to the Pivka garrison, and my assignment there was commander of the 2nd Motorised Company, in the 1st Battalion of the 228th Motorised Brigade. I was there from March 1986.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, before you had been mobilised to Pivka, you had been told to deploy to special forces that were bound for Kosovo. I think you told us that in direct-examination. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that I was to be deployed to the Postojna garrison, the battalion for -- as company commander, and the units which would be is sent to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In refusing you that assignment, you told us, on page 17824 to 17825, that you were told that on four separate occasions that you were insubordinate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I apologise, but I got the interpretation that I was insubordinate in four different situations. Now, I don't know what the question actually was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Were you told on four different occasions that your refusal to take this assignment was an act of insubordination?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What I was told -- would you please allow me to look at my notes so I can see what I was exactly told, if that is the question, if you want to know what I was told on those four occasions?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Try to be more direct, Mr. Prosecutor. Get to your questions more directly, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony, and I'm reading from page 17824 and 25, in your refusal to take this assignment, General, you noted that your superiors said that this would be an act of disobedience and insubordination and, "I could be sanctioned for it." Do you recall saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I found it, except here in the transcript it says, "Commander of the 14th Regiment said that this was insubordination and that I was going to be sanctioned for it."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this was in 1985, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: End of 1985, early 1986. Between December of 1985 and early 1986.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were never punished for that act of insubordination, were you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was never punished in the former JNA, period, both during the period when I was a cadet and later on when I was a commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, General, within a year of your insubordination you received a review from the JNA where you were evaluated with special distinction; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know when I received this. I don't know whether that was a proposal. It was, I think, an evaluation but on the basis of -- but I was sent to the Pivka garrison instead of Postojna because of my refusal to go to Kosovo. Later on, I was never sent to Kosovo, it was never even proposed to go to Kosovo, even though my colleagues from the brigade were sent down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you refused for the forces to go to Kosovo, and within a year, you received a review with special distinction. Would you agree with me that your officers, your superior officers, thought that you were an outstanding officer; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what they thought, but what they thought they must have written down in the official review.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that in 1986, you went to the Pivka garrison. Now, what was your job in the Pivka garrison in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the Pivka garrison in Slovenia, I took the duty of the commander of the 2nd Motorised Company in the 1st Motorised Battalion in the 228th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your job there, sir, when you were in the Pivka garrison specifically?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My duty was the training of soldiers of the 2nd Motorised Company in this 1st Motorised Battalion. I had the duty of commander of the motorised company, and I can explain exactly what this position involved. If this is the question, I can say what the duties covered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's try to focus the discussion here. The witness suggested that he would make the question more specific, but was that, in fact, your question, Mr. Prosecutor? What I'm afraid of sometimes is that we seem to be drifting away from our proper direction. I can tell you, Mr. Kehoe, and with all the respect that I have for you, that you cannot have one more minute for your cross-examination than has been planned. Therefore, you have to be the one to choose your questions. Sometimes I have the impression that we're moving away from where we should be. Between you, who asks very long, complicated questions, and the witness, who answers, it's his right, of course, but in a long way, I can repeat to you that there's not going to be one extra minute granted for the cross-examination. Was it important to know that the witness would give specifications about all of these responses? Because if we reconstitute all of the elements of his military career, every act and gesture that he made, I'm afraid that at some point we're not going to get anywhere. You know, Mr. Kehoe, when you've reached the end of the time, you always say you have another 15 or 20 questions, and then you'll have to give them up regrettably. I want to tell you this now, that is, from the very beginning of the cross-examination, so let's be sure we understand one another on that subject. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll carve the questions down as sharply as I possibly can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Specifically, General, you noted that you were an officer in the battalion in charge of morale. Do you recall that testimony during direct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I recall it. Later on, in the subsequent period, I was transferred from the duty of the commander of the company. In other words, I gave that duty up and took over another duty which comprised two duties. One was the deputy commander of the battalion and assistant commander for morale.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'd like to make the comment to you, General Blaskic. Try to answer concretely. As regards the rights of the accused, you know that the Judges are very conscious of those rights, but I would like to ask you to try to answer the questions. The question that the Prosecutor asked was very precise. "Were you involved with morale?" If you have to explain why and how and this and that, unless, of course, it is really essential to your answer, please don't. I'm afraid that we're wasting some time at the start of this cross-examination. I know that I'm using time as well, but we will have to try to make up the time later on. Therefore, we want to know if you were involved in troop morale. I suppose that you were, at least that's what you said in your examination-in-chief. All that was said. Judge Rodrigues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Jorda. Before we continue, General Blaskic, I would like to ask you a question. I believe that I remember that the commander, after you refused to go to Kosovo, put you at the Pivka garrison, and I believe that I remember that the commander of that Pivka garrison made a comment to you when you arrived. I have this in my mind. I think he asked you, "What did you do wrong in order to be sent here?" I have this thought in my mind. Could you tell us whether there was that sort of a comment and what it was actually?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. You do recall it very well indeed. I also recall that meeting. For me, it was a shock of sorts because this chief, he was the chief of staff of the 228th Motorised Brigade in Pivka. He was the lieutenant colonel, and his name was Dusan Reljanovic. I put on my parade uniform. It was my first day there. I saluted him, and when I greeted him, he said, "What did you do wrong to be sent over here to us?" At the time, as the chief of staff of the brigade, he was actually an acting deputy commander of the 228th Motorised Brigade, and I think the commander's name was Kasim Smajlbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Prosecutor, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in your role as being involved in the morale of the actual battalion, did that involve also being involved in the political affairs and politics?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was on this duty for a very short period of time and had not completed the course, which was compulsory for all officers because it was the political situation at the time in Yugoslavia. My duty was assistant for morale, so the focus of my duty was dissemination of information and the lifting of morale of the soldiers. So if there was something that we needed to convey from the news that was being brought from the government, I would do it once a week. In other words, I would summarise the news, the current news situation which I gained from the mass media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the role of the political officer in the battalion was to instruct the military units of the politics of the communist party; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Until 1989, until the communist party broke up, this duty for morale had not existed. I think that until then, it was the assistant commander for the political affairs, but when the Communist Party of Yugoslavia broke up - I think that there was a congress which they had in 1989 - I think that this duty was then phased out, and there was no assistant commander for political affairs at the battalion level. In fact, this ushered the multi-party system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, were you or were you not for the last eleven months of your career in the JNA the assistant commander for political affairs?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would have to look to find this order of appointment, but I know that I was assistant commander for morale and I was the deputy commander. Those were my official duties. I was the assistant commander for the building of morale among troops and the deputy commander. I was not the assistant commander for political affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you a document then, General. If I may also give you another document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, did I give you enough copies of this other document? I don't believe I have. There should be a cover letter from the Federal Ministry of Justice in Belgrade, as well as a document for the personnel department. In BCS, it's one page, and in the English translation, it is two.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document, which is not translated, will have the number 576, and the second will be 577 and 577A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Registrar, there are copies for that first document in English. I neglected to give them to the usher. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 577 will also have a second number which will be 577A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think that was 576. I'm a little confused on your ordering. The document dated the 4th of May, 1998, that should go with the document that has the numbering in it 1 through 5 in the centre. That's right. What number is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 576 for the original and 576A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first document is the letter sent to the Ministry of Defence on the General's record in the JNA. The cover letter is in Cyrillic and in English. The next document is the actual report that was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by General Zoric, Dusan Zoric of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're more than welcome, General, to read this entire document concerning your career, noted 1 through 5, but in number 5 of this document, it notes that you were the motorised battalion assistant commander for political affairs, at the same time deputy commander, for 11 months; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's begin. Are you talking about 576 here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We are talking about 576, which is the document that is information concerning General Blaskic's career in the then JNA, now designated the Yugoslav army. They talk about his military career, and in point 5 of that it describes the General as the assistant commander for political affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Yes, I see. All right. What's the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the question, General, is that the assistant commander for political affairs is significantly different than what you told this Trial Chamber that you were just in charge of morale; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that it is significantly different, but I was never assistant commander for political affairs in the battalion. I received the order of appointment. I signed it. I was given it in the Postojna garrison, and I was told that the duty was the assistant commander for morale and deputy commander. At that time, when I was there, the duty of the assistant commander for political affairs had been dissolved because it did not exist at that time in the history of the JNA. There are further errors here because it says I was reviewed in 1986. That is not correct. I was reviewed in 1987. Then it says that I was reviewed in 1989. That is also not correct. I was reviewed in 1990, on the 30th of July, 1990. That is when I received my official review, not in 1989. Further, in this document -- just a moment, please. My mother's name is incorrect. She was not Komsic. I applied for my -- tendered my resignation on 12 August, and I think that the date shown here is probably when my case was actually decided on. It is also not true that I was the commander of a platoon for two years. I received an order appointing me the commander of cadet training of the 14th Proletarian Brigade. I was not commander of the rifleman platoon -- Rifle Platoon commander, and I never received that duty. I don't know how it ended up here. Number 3, I did receive an order appointing me to the Motorised Company, acting commanding officer in Pivka, and this order was communicated to me. Number 5, I was not Motorised Battalion assistant commander for political affairs. I never was given a document appointing me to that duty and I never signed such an order. So I was assistant commander for morale and, at the same time, deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the document speaks for itself, Mr. President. Let us talk, General, about your commanders in Pivka. Who was your commander when you were at the Pivka garrison?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't remember his name. Captain First Class Stankovic, and he later became a Major. In Pivka, when I came, the previous commander had committed suicide, and before him, the commander of the battalion also attempted suicide, so that there were frequent replacements. Later on, when I came, it was Captain First Class, I think his name was Mlodrag Stankovic. The commander of the brigade was Colonel Kasim Smajlbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to Captain Stankovic? Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Before taking up his duties as battalion commander, he told me that he was a clerk for sport in the division of the 14th Proletarian, and after the duty of commander of the battalion he received the rank of Major, and he performed some sort of duty in the operative and instructors' department of the command of the 228th Motorised Brigade in Pivka and in Postojna. I don't know his specific duties. But Stankovic is a surname which is fairly frequent, and that is why I said I think that his name was Mlodrag, because I know that there were many people with the surname Stankovic. Usually it was Stankovic, Petrovic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if he fought on one side during the war?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that he was married in Slovenia. His wife was from the Republic of Slovenia. I'm sure of that. She was a Slovene. I don't know whether he fought or not, but I can only suppose that if he lived with his family in Postojna that he remained in Postojna, but those are my assumptions. I really don't have any information on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was Bosko Peulic your superior?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was, as far as I know, first the commander of the battalion in Vipava, and he was the next commander after Captain First Class Stankovic. Quite possibly this could have been in 1987 or 1988. I am sure that he was for a time in 1988, but I don't know exactly when the commanders of the battalions replaced one another because there was more. There was several. As I say, this was -- they were -- took each other's place fairly often. They were changed fairly frequently, but he was one too at some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Peulic fought for the VRS during the war, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He fought for the army of the Republika Srpska during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 528. Take a look at Exhibit 528. That is, in fact, the same Bosko Peulic who is the Lieutenant Colonel of the 27th Motorised Brigade for the VRS, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps we should take a ten-minute break which will allow General Blaskic the time to familiarise himself with the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We'll resume the hearing now. I suppose that you familiarised yourself with the document, that is, Prosecution document 528. It is a Prosecution document; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, 528. There is no version in French. The one that's in English on the ELMO, how does that work? I'll give it to my colleagues here. It's the only version that we have. All right. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we know that Bosko Peulic fought for the VSR during the war. Do you know of other Serb associates from the JNA, General, who fought for the VRS?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have, from the former JNA, my former colleagues, so to speak, but I have not contacted with them since I left the JNA and with some of them since I was taken prisoner in 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, those are the colleagues I'm talking about. Those colleagues -- you did have colleagues that fought for the VRS. Who were they, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "colleagues." I had colleagues who were associates of mine previously, whom I worked together with. When I left, however, when I left the JNA, I stopped all contact with them and they were no longer my colleagues and friends, if that's what you mean. I don't know what you actually mean when you say "colleagues."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs that you served with and that you knew when you were with the JNA, did any of these Serbs fight for the VRS around the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, your area of command? If so, who?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Now this is clear to me. So you mean the Serbs who served in the JNA with me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Did they take part on the other side? Just one moment, because the zone is a large one. According to what I know, there was Bosko Peulic, and I also knew a Major, Balcojkic, but I don't know exactly what duty he performed on the side of the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have contact with either one of these men while you were in the HVO or, specifically, during 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never contacted them. I never had contacts with them. According to my instructions, orders, neither did any of my associates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, did associates and units under your command fight in concert with Bosko Peulic in the Zepce area? Specifically we're talking about June of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1993, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. At that time I was cut off in the Lasva pocket. It is possible that there was fighting in Zepce but I'm not sure. Perhaps Bosko Peulic was up there at that time but, as I say, at the time I myself was in the Lasva pocket, I was not in Zepce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, did you ever learn of HVO units under your command fighting in concert with VRS units under the command of Bosko Peulic? Did you ever learn about that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I heard about it. It was a propaganda news item used by the BH army relating to co-operation and so forth. So I did hear something of the kind, but I said that according to my orders, that was not done. I was in the Lasva pocket from the 16th of April, 1993, and I could not have physically been in Zepce. Zepce directly communicated with the main staff of the HVO, and I didn't know that there was collaboration with the army of Republika Srpska in the sense of communication, in the sense of seeing to the wounded, logistic supplies for Zepce, and so on and so forth, but not following my instructions or orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, the brigade commander in the Zepce area was Ivo Livancic, and that is an individual that we have noted his name in numerous correspondence that the Defence has introduced; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was a man called Ivo Lozancic, but I underline that from the 16th of April I was in the Lasva pocket and I was not physically present up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, at any point up till now, after the Washington Accords and up till now, did you talk to Ivo Lozancic and ask him whether or not he was operating jointly with the VRS in Zepce?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the signing of the Washington Accords, possibly I did discuss matters of this kind with him but, once again, I tell you I was aware of that information, that is to say, that a form of co-operation had got under way, but I repeat, not on my orders and not on my instructions. So I did not order Lozancic to hold those forms of co-operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what did Lozancic tell you about his co-operation with the VRS?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That he told me, after the Washington Accords, that they attended to the wounded in Banja Luka, HVO injured persons, because there was no hospital in Zepce at the time, and that food also came into the region, and complete aid and assistance by a ground corridor under the supervision of the army of Republika Srpska and that all that was paid for through commercial accounts. All this assistance was paid for, in fact. I also know that there were contacts linked to mediation by the international organisations when it came to an exchange of information as to missing persons, as to detained persons, or an exchange of the corpses of those who had been killed, but that was prior to these forms of co-operation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to this at a later time, General. Let me go back to your career. When you left the JNA in 1991, you were eligible to take the Major's exam, I think you said, but the Major's exam was never given because of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's not correct. I did attend a Major's examination but I only sat for one examination, not the whole set of examinations, and I never passed my Major's examination. I think that in 1990 I had the necessary conditions to sit for the Major's examinations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, General. We're going to talk a little bit about your career in the HVO. We will not talk about the early part of your career, because we'll do that in some detail in a little bit, but I would like to ask you some questions at the outset from the time frame when you became the deputy chief of staff of the HVO until the time where you were promoted to the HV, and specifically you noted for us, during your direct-examination, that you were promoted to the deputy chief of staff on the 6th of approximately May of 1994. You delayed taking that position but you ultimately took the position sometime in May of 1994. My question for you is: When you took the deputy chief of staff position, who was the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The chief of staff was General Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did Petkovic stay in that position as the chief of staff? Did he stay until you received the chief of staff position in August of 1994?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He was in that duty until August. I think, 5th or 6th of August, '94.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, when you came as deputy chief of staff to the HVO, who was the HVO representative to the federation army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean when I became the chief of staff or deputy chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for any miscommunication, but I believe my question was when you were deputy chief of staff, who was the HVO representative to the federation army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it was General Ante Roso.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is the Ante Roso that originally gave you your promotion or gave you your rank on the 27th of July, 1992, gave you your rank of Lieutenant Colonel; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I had said how I was given this rank. It was not on the 27th of June but the 27th of July, 1992, and this document was signed by Mr. Mate Boban and General Roso.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this is the same Ante Roso; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did Roso stay in the position as the head of the federation army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how long but I know who replaced him. I do not know. I really don't know that piece of information, how long he stayed in that duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who replaced him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was Brigadier Zivko Budimir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did Zivko Budimir stay in that position as head of the HVO contingent to the federation army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Neither of them were the chief of the HVO within the federation army. He was the deputy chief of the HVO, both Roso and Budimir, and the chief of the HVO in the federation army was the chief of staff -- the commander of the HVO, and Zivko Budimir stayed there until sometime in November or December of 1995. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, you became the chief of staff, I think you told us, on the 6th of August, 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your deputy chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For a brief period of time, it was Brigadier Nedeljko Obradovic, but again I don't know exactly for how long a period, and then it was Brigadier Milenko Lasic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did Zarko Tole serve under you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, he never served under me, that is, if I understood the question correctly, Your Honours, when was Zarko Tole my subordinate. He was never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was never your subordinate at any time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if he was your subordinate, would you know?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that in point of fact this man was never my subordinate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come back to that in due course, General. My question ending this area has to do with your promotion to the HV. Now, you received this notification that you were promoted from chief of staff of the HVO and the federation army to the HV. When did that occur?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This was in November 1995. I was informed that this order came that I was promoted to the HV General, and I was appointed inspector in the chief inspectorate of the HV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who issued that order taking you or ordering you into the HV from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This order was read on HTV, Croatian Television. I don't know who signed it. I know that it came from the commander in chief of the armed forces of Croatia, President Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you never saw a written order ordering you to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina and to go to the Republic of Croatia? You never received any document telling you what to do?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw this document but I'm not sure whether somebody had signed it on behalf of the commander in chief, but I did see this document. This document was shown on television, but I saw the document itself also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The signature line at the bottom of this document, according to your testimony, was that of President Franjo Tudjman; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I said that I am not sure who had signed the document but that I did see that President Tudjman's name was typewritten as commander in chief, but I don't know who actually signed it, whether it was somebody from the personnel on his behalf or something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, was that a common occurrence in the HVO, for officers in the HVO to be promoted to the army of another country, the Republic of Croatia? Was that common?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if that was a usual thing. I know that for awhile you could apply. You could apply for a request for active duty and then receive a reply whether you were accepted to the HV. For awhile, the HV did accept officers based on the requests, on applications. I'm not sure whether you think that this was just a regular procedure. Everybody had to apply, in other words, send a formal request to be accepted, admitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you told us in direct examination that this appointment to the HV came to you as a complete surprise. That's what you told us in response to questions by Mr. Nobilo. Did you apply to be a General in the HV?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally did not submit an application, but President Zubak, who was my superior, who was commander in chief, he was with the delegation in Dayton, and I don't know how my appointment came about. I said what happened and what I knew and what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, General, is is it normal for a president of one country to order the officer of another country to report to this second army? Is that a normal course of events based on your career in the HV and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, an objection regarding the way the question is posed because it suggests something that the witness never said. He said that President Tudjman had appointed him into the HV, but he did not say that this is a document by which he was transferred from the HVO to the HV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I understand what you're saying, Mr. Nobilo, but I think that the question was not quite that. Mr. Kehoe was asking a question in his way of asking it.
